In the Sehore government school, Vikas's father owned the rice mill, and Vikas never let anyone forget it. On Monday he picked up Madhav's dented tin geometry box and rattled it. "Cheap stuff. Mine's imported, see? Magnetic." A few boys laughed.
Madhav's face went hot. He grabbed the box back and stared at his desk. He wanted to shout that his father had bought it with a whole day's wages.
Instead he got up and went to the mango tree, where Salim and Kamla were sharing roasted chana. "Sit," Kamla said, and poured some into his palm.
Later, Madhav noticed something. Vikas bragged loudest on the days tests came back. Today he had got four out of twenty. Maybe the shiny box was all he had to feel good about.

qa.q: What did Vikas say about his own geometry box?
qa.a: That it was imported and magnetic.

qa.q: How did Madhav feel when the boys laughed?
qa.a: Ashamed and angry; his face went hot and he wanted to shout.

qa.q: What did Madhav choose instead of shouting, and why was it wise?
qa.a: He walked away to the mango tree and sat with kinder friends, which avoided a fight and kept him among people who valued him.

qa.q: What might be behind Vikas's bragging?
qa.a: Insecurity; he bragged loudest on test days and had scored four out of twenty, so the shiny box may have been his way to feel good.

grounding: A boy shamed by a richer classmate's bragging walks away to kinder friends and sees that the bragging shows the other boy's insecurity, not his own worth.

At the school gate in São Paulo, Rafael held up his new phone so everyone could see. Then he pointed at Yara's, with its cracked corner and stickers. "What is that, a brick? My grandmother has a better one."
A few kids snickered. Yara shoved her phone into her pocket, cheeks burning. Her brother had passed it down to her, and until that moment she had loved it.
She opened her mouth to say something mean about Rafael's ears. Then she closed it, turned around and walked to the bench where Beatriz was drawing. "Can I see?" Beatriz slid the sketchbook over.
From there Yara watched Rafael showing the phone to one group, then another, as if he needed every single person to be impressed. It didn't look like fun. It looked tiring.

qa.q: What did Rafael call Yara's phone?
qa.a: A brick.

qa.q: What was Yara feeling when the kids snickered?
qa.a: Ashamed and embarrassed; her cheeks burned and she hid the phone she had loved.

qa.q: What did Yara do instead of insulting Rafael back?
qa.a: She walked away and sat with Beatriz, a kinder friend.

qa.q: What does Rafael's need to show the phone to group after group suggest?
qa.a: That he may need everyone's admiration to feel okay, which points to his insecurity rather than to Yara's worth.

grounding: A girl mocked by a wealthier classmate for her old phone feels ashamed, walks away to a kinder friend and sees the bragging as his insecurity.

The notice for the class trip to the science centre in Hyderabad said ₹600, due Friday. Everyone in Rekha's class was buzzing. Rekha folded the notice very small and pushed it to the bottom of her bag. That week her mother had been counting coins for the electricity bill.
When classmates asked, she said, "I don't like museums. Boring." Her face felt hot.
On Thursday Jagdish Sir asked her to stay back for a minute. The classroom was empty. "Rekha, I haven't got your slip. Is something making it hard?"
She stared at the floor, then nodded.
"Thank you for telling me," he said quietly. "The school has a small fund for exactly this. Nobody else needs to know. Take this form to your mother."
Rekha walked out lighter. On Monday she sat by the bus window like everyone else.

qa.q: How much did the trip cost?
qa.a: ₹600, due Friday.

qa.q: Why did Rekha say museums were boring?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed that her family could not afford the trip and wanted to hide it.

qa.q: How did Jagdish Sir handle it wisely?
qa.a: He spoke to her privately, thanked her for telling him and quietly offered the school fund.

qa.q: How does Jagdish Sir see Rekha's situation?
qa.a: As a practical problem to solve quietly, not something for her to be ashamed of.

grounding: A girl embarrassed that she cannot afford a class trip talks privately to a teacher, who finds quiet help.

"Yogesh, your picnic form is blank. Aren't you coming?"
"No, Ma'am. I'll have a stomach ache that day."
"The picnic is two weeks away."
"It'll... come early."
Gopika Ma'am smiled a little, then lowered her voice. "Is it the money?"
Yogesh's ears burned. He nodded at the floor. "Papa's shop was shut all month. I didn't want anyone to know."
"There's nothing shameful in that. Money is a grown-up worry, not yours to carry."
"But the others will find out."
"They won't. The school has a quiet fund. I'll call your father myself tonight, and you'll hand in a form like everyone else."
"Really?"
"Really. And Yogesh? What you're worth has nothing to do with money."
He grinned for the first time that day.

qa.q: Why was Yogesh's family short of money?
qa.a: Papa's shop was shut all month.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when Gopika Ma'am asked about the money?
qa.a: He felt ashamed; his ears burned and he looked at the floor.

qa.q: What did Gopika Ma'am offer, and why was it kind?
qa.a: The school's quiet fund and a call to his father that night, so he could come without anyone knowing.

qa.q: How does Gopika Ma'am see Yogesh's worry?
qa.a: As a grown-up money worry he should not have to carry, and nothing to be ashamed of.

grounding: A boy ashamed that he cannot afford a school picnic is helped privately by a teacher who reminds him his worth does not depend on money.

Papa's office friends had come for Sunday lunch at their Bengaluru flat. When Thomas Uncle, the family driver, carried in the heavy boxes of sweets from the car, one guest pointed without looking up. "Put it there. And get ice."
Thomas Uncle nodded and went to the kitchen. Nobody said thank you.
Mahima felt a small, hot twist in her stomach. Thomas Uncle drove her to school every day and knew all her friends' names. His daughter Merin was in Class 3.
She followed him into the kitchen. "Thank you for carrying all that, Uncle. Is Merin's tooth out yet?"
He laughed. "Yesterday! She put it under her pillow."
When she went back, she set a glass of cold water on the table for him too. Papa noticed, and gave her a small nod.

qa.q: Who is Merin?
qa.a: Thomas Uncle's daughter, who is in Class 3.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when nobody thanked Thomas Uncle?
qa.a: A small, hot twist of discomfort, because she felt he deserved respect.

qa.q: How did Mahima show respect to Thomas Uncle?
qa.a: She thanked him, asked after Merin and set out a glass of cold water for him too.

qa.q: How might Thomas Uncle have felt when Mahima asked about Merin?
qa.a: Seen and cheered; he laughed and shared the tooth story.

grounding: When visitors treat the family driver as lesser, a girl thanks him and remembers he is a parent too.

"Oye, water lao!" Jatin shouted towards the kitchen, not looking up from his game.
His cousin Tarun put down his comic. "Her name is Savitri Didi."
"So? She's the cook."
"So say her name. And please."
Jatin rolled his eyes. "At my house nobody says please to servants."
Savitri Didi came out wiping her hands, two glasses on a tray. Tarun stood and took one. "Thank you, Didi. Did Chotu pass his maths test?"
Her face softened. "Passed, beta! Sixty-eight marks."
"Tell him well done from me."
When she had gone, Jatin muttered, "You know her son's marks?"
"She's been with us since I was born. She's someone's mother, same as yours."
Jatin was quiet. Later, when she brought the pakoras, he mumbled, "Thank you... Didi."

qa.q: How many marks did Chotu get in maths?
qa.a: Sixty-eight marks.

qa.q: Why did Tarun put his comic down when Jatin shouted?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable at Jatin's rudeness and wanted Savitri Didi treated with respect.

qa.q: How did Tarun teach Jatin without a fight?
qa.a: By using her name, thanking her himself, and pointing out that she is someone's mother, just like Jatin's.

qa.q: How might Savitri Didi have felt when Tarun asked about Chotu?
qa.a: Respected and warm; her face softened and she proudly shared his marks.

grounding: A boy shows respect to the family cook by using her name and thanking her, and reminds his cousin that she is someone's parent too.

On the way to school, Pankaj's bus stopped at the big signal, and a small girl in a torn frock tapped on the window, holding out her palm. She looked younger than his sister. The bus moved on before he could do anything.
All morning he couldn't stop seeing her face. In moral science period he put up his hand. "Ma'am, there's a girl at the signal. Can we help her?"
Gurpreet Ma'am didn't brush it away. "It's good that it tugged at you. What might be safe ways to help?"
The class made a list: ask parents first, keep biscuits or fruit in the car instead of handing things out alone, and support groups that run shelters and classes for such children.
That evening Pankaj asked his father about the children's shelter near the bus depot. They signed up to donate books on Sunday.

qa.q: What did the girl at the signal hold out?
qa.a: Her palm.

qa.q: What did Pankaj feel after seeing the girl?
qa.a: A tug of compassion and worry; he could not stop seeing her face all morning.

qa.q: What safe ways to help did the class list?
qa.a: Ask parents first, keep biscuits or fruit in the car, and support groups that run shelters and classes.

qa.q: How does Gurpreet Ma'am see Pankaj's question?
qa.a: As a good sign of his compassion, which she turns into a class discussion about safe ways to help.

grounding: A boy moved by a child begging at a signal asks adults about safe ways to help, like giving food or supporting an organisation.

Tuesday: At the Andheri signal, a boy about Nandini's age knocked on the car window, pointing to his mouth. Nandini grabbed her purse. "Mummy, can I give him my money?" The light turned green before Mummy could answer. Nandini's chest felt heavy all the way home.

Mummy also began keeping small packets of fruit in the car. The next Monday, at the same signal, Nandini handed one through the window with both hands. The boy smiled.

qa.a: At the Andheri signal.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel all the way home on Tuesday?
qa.a: Heavy-hearted and sad, wanting to help the boy but unable to.

qa.q: What safe ways to help did the family choose?
qa.a: Donating books and rice to the children's centre and keeping fruit packets in the car to hand out.

qa.q: How might the boy at the signal have felt when Nandini handed him the fruit with both hands?
qa.a: Treated with respect; he smiled.

In the school lunch hall, Aparna opened her steel box: two dry rotis and a pinch of salt. It had been a tight month at home. She angled the lid so nobody could see.
Abhinav slid into the seat beside her with his three-tier tiffin. Without a word, he pushed the middle tier, paneer and peas, halfway between them and began eating from his side as if that were normal.
Aparna's cheeks warmed. She felt thankful and a bit awkward all at once. Was it pity? But Abhinav was only talking about the cricket match, not looking at her rotis at all.
"Thanks," she said quietly, and tore a roti to share with him.
The next day she brought guavas from the tree behind her house, salted and cut, and put the best half on his lid.

qa.q: What was in the middle tier Abhinav shared?
qa.a: Paneer and peas.

qa.q: What did Aparna feel when Abhinav pushed the tier over?
qa.a: Grateful and a bit awkward at the same time, wondering whether it was pity.

qa.q: How did Aparna respond in a way that kept the friendship equal?
qa.a: She accepted warmly, shared her roti, and the next day brought guavas to share with him.

qa.q: How does Abhinav seem to see sharing his tiffin?
qa.a: As something normal between friends, not a favour; he made no show of it.

grounding: A girl whose richer friend shares his tiffin without fuss feels grateful and awkward, accepts warmly and shares something of her own.

His friend Kartik, whose family owned the sweet shop, quietly tore his big cheese sandwich in two and put half on Rafiq's napkin. "Too much for me." He didn't look at the bun at all. Rafiq said thanks, but his neck felt hot.
Tuesday: Kartik did it again. This time Rafiq pushed it back. "I'm not hungry." His stomach growled loudly. Kartik shrugged, but looked a little hurt.
Thursday: The night before, Rafiq had rolled extra shami kebabs with Ammi and his sister Ishita. At lunch he opened his box and pushed it to the middle. "Ammi's kebabs. Your turn to share." Kartik grinned and set his sandwich beside them. They ate from both, trading bites and cricket scores.

qa.a: The sweet shop.

qa.q: Why did Rafiq push the sandwich back on Tuesday?
qa.a: He felt awkward and proud, uncomfortable taking help again even though he was hungry.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do on Thursday that made accepting easier?
qa.a: He brought Ammi's kebabs to share, so both boys gave and received.

qa.q: How might Kartik have felt when Rafiq refused on Tuesday?

grounding: A boy whose richer friend quietly shares his lunch feels grateful but awkward, and learns to accept warmly and share something of his own in return.

At the village school near Barabanki, a group of older boys waited for Farhan by the hand pump every day. Today they blocked his way and chanted a nasty name about his religion, laughing when he tried to pass.
Lalit, filling his bottle, felt his hands clench. Farhan sat next to him in class and shared his eraser without being asked. This was wrong.
Lalit didn't shout at the boys. He walked over, stood beside Farhan and said, "Come, the bell's going." Together they walked away.
At lunch he sat with Farhan under the peepal tree. Farhan said, "It happens every day." That settled it. After lunch Lalit went to Pandey Sir. Sir listened, called both boys in to hear Farhan's side, and spoke to the older boys' class before the last bell. "Tell me at once if it happens again," he said.

qa.q: Where did the older boys wait for Farhan?
qa.a: By the hand pump.

qa.q: What did Lalit feel when he saw the boys chanting?
qa.a: Angry; his hands clenched because he knew it was wrong.

qa.q: What steps did Lalit take, and why were they wise?
qa.a: He stood beside Farhan and walked away with him, sat with him at lunch, and told Pandey Sir, who acted that same day.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Lalit stood beside him?
qa.a: Less alone, and relieved to have someone on his side after facing it every day.

grounding: A boy who sees a classmate called names for his religion feels angry, sits with him and tells a teacher, who acts that day.

At Lindiwe's school in Leeds, the new boy Kwame had moved from Accra in January. Whenever he answered a question, two boys at the back copied his accent in silly voices, and half the class sniggered.
On Wednesday it happened during reading. Kwame's voice got smaller and smaller until he stopped mid-sentence and sat down.
Lindiwe felt heat rise up her neck. Her own gran spoke with a Zulu accent, and Lindiwe would have hated anyone laughing at her.
At break she carried her snack over and sat beside Kwame on the wall. "Your reading was good. They're just being silly." He shrugged, but stayed.
Before lunch she went to Mr. Hughes and told him what had been happening. He thanked her, spoke to the two boys that afternoon, and asked Kwame if he would like to tell the class about Accra on Friday.

qa.q: Where had Kwame moved from?
qa.a: Accra.

qa.q: What did Lindiwe feel when Kwame stopped mid-sentence?
qa.a: Angry, with heat rising up her neck, and protective, because she thought of her gran.

qa.q: What two things did Lindiwe do to help?
qa.a: She sat with Kwame at break and told Mr. Hughes, who spoke to the boys that afternoon.

qa.q: How might Kwame have felt when his voice got smaller during reading?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt, wanting to disappear from the laughter.

At Midsummer lunch in Grandma's garden outside Uppsala, Uncle Lars put down his fork and started one of his speeches. "People from those countries just come here for handouts. They don't want to work." A few adults nodded. Someone passed the potatoes.
Astrid's stomach turned. Her best friend Tuan's parents ran the bakery on her street and were up at four every morning. She said nothing, but she didn't nod either. She stared at her plate.
After lunch, while the others played croquet, she helped Grandma carry cups inside. "Grandma, why does Uncle Lars think that?"
Grandma sighed and dried her hands. "I think he's scared about his own job, and it's easier to blame strangers. You're right to wonder. What do you think?"
"I think he doesn't know Tuan's family."
"Then maybe one day you can tell him about them," Grandma said.

qa.q: What did Tuan's parents run?
qa.a: The bakery on Astrid's street.

qa.q: Why did Astrid's stomach turn at the lunch?
qa.a: She felt uneasy and upset, because Uncle Lars's words did not match the hard-working family she knew.

qa.q: What did Astrid do instead of arguing at the table?
qa.a: She quietly did not nod, then asked Grandma in private why Uncle Lars thought that.

qa.q: Why might Uncle Lars talk this way, according to Grandma?
qa.a: He may be scared about his own job and find it easier to blame strangers.

grounding: A girl uneasy when an older relative speaks badly about a group quietly holds her own view and later asks a trusted elder why.

In the clinic waiting room, Noor sat between her Phuphi and her cousin Hafsa. When a nurse called the next name, Phuphi leaned over and whispered loudly, "Look, one of those people. Their kind are never clean. I hope she doesn't touch me." Hafsa nodded as if it were ordinary.
Noor looked at the nurse. She had gentle hands and had just helped an old man with his walking stick. Noor's stomach went tight. She didn't nod.
That night she sat by Nani. "Nani, why does Phuphi talk like that about some people?"
Nani said, "Some grown-ups learned those ideas when they were small and never questioned them. It is not right. You can keep your own view, and be kind to everyone."
Next visit, Noor decided, she would smile at that nurse.

qa.q: How did Noor feel when Phuphi whispered about the nurse?

qa.q: How did Noor hold her own view without a fight?
qa.a: She did not nod along, then later asked Nani, a trusted elder, why Phuphi talks that way.

"Asif, are you crying? Over a football match?" Anirban laughed. "Boys don't cry, yaar."
Asif wiped his face fast. "I'm not crying. It's sweat."
"Sweat from your eyes?"
"We lost the final by one goal! I missed the penalty!"
"So? My dad says crying is for girls."
Asif sat down on the bench. "Why, though? Who made that rule?"
Anirban opened his mouth, then shut it. "I don't know. Everyone says it."
"My Abbu cried when my baby sister was born. He's not weak."
Anirban scuffed the ground. "Okay. I cried when my dog died. Don't tell anyone."
"I won't." Asif laughed wetly. "Next year we'll win and cry about that too."
"Deal," Anirban said, and sat down beside him.

qa.q: By how much did they lose the final?
qa.a: By one goal.

qa.q: Why did Asif say it was just sweat?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about crying after Anirban laughed at him.

qa.q: What did Asif do that challenged the rule?
qa.a: He asked who made the rule and pointed out that his Abbu cried and is not weak.

qa.q: How did Anirban's view change during the talk?
qa.a: He realised he did not know why the rule existed, admitted he had cried too, and sat beside Asif.

grounding: A boy told that boys should not cry questions who made the rule and finds a friend who accepts him.

I'm Payal, and last summer our building's cricket team needed a bowler. I've been bowling at the wall since I was small. But when I walked onto the terrace pitch, Sharma Uncle from the fourth floor called out, "Cricket is for boys, beti. Go and play with the girls."
My face went hot. It felt so unfair. I bowl faster than half of them!
I almost went home. Then Manoj, the captain, tossed me the ball. "Uncle, just watch one over."
I took three wickets. Sharma Uncle clapped, a bit grudgingly.
That night I asked Mummy why people say that. She said some rules are just old habits nobody ever questioned. I'm still bowling. I'm the team's opening bowler now.

qa.q: How many wickets did Payal take in the over?
qa.a: Three wickets.

qa.q: How did Payal feel when Sharma Uncle said cricket is for boys?
qa.a: Hurt and angry; it felt unfair, and Payal's face went hot.

qa.q: What helped Payal keep doing what Payal loves?
qa.a: Manoj's support, proving it in one over, and asking Mummy why people say such things.

qa.q: How might Sharma Uncle have seen things after the over?
qa.a: He had to admit Payal could play, clapping even if grudgingly.

grounding: A girl told that cricket is for boys feels it is unfair, keeps playing with a friend's support and asks why the rule exists.

passage:
Value-education period note, Class 5
During our talk on fairness, Mehak raised her hand slowly. "At my aunt's house, Kamla Didi, the cook, has to drink tea from a separate glass kept outside. Why?" Her voice was shaky, and she looked confused and sad. Bhavna said, "Ours too," and a few children went quiet.
I did not shame anyone's family. I said that treating a person as less clean because of their work or their birth is not fair, and that many families are learning to change old habits. I suggested Mehak talk to her parents about it gently at home.
After class Mehak told me that she wants to share her own glasses with Kamla Didi when she visits. I have sent a note to her parents about our discussion.

qa.q: Where was Kamla Didi's separate glass kept?
qa.a: Outside, at Mehak's aunt's house.

qa.q: How did Mehak seem when she asked her question?
qa.a: Confused and sad; her voice was shaky.

qa.q: How did the teacher handle the question?
qa.a: They explained that treating someone as less clean for their work or birth is unfair, without shaming families, and suggested Mehak talk to her parents gently.

qa.q: How might Kamla Didi feel being given a separate glass?
qa.a: Hurt and humiliated, treated as less than the family she works for.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a girl confused and sad at seeing a cook given a separate glass, and how asking her parents about fairness is a start.

I'm Uday. In Class 5, a new boy called Joel joined our section. He hummed while he worked and flapped his hands when he got excited about trains. My friends thought he was weird. Urmila said, "If anyone sits with Joel, they can't sit with us." Everyone agreed. I agreed too, out loud. Inside I felt sick and scared. I didn't want to be alone at lunch.

qa.a: Saying hi at the gate, lending the blue pen and sitting with Joel in library period.

qa.q: How might Joel have experienced Uday's small kindnesses?
qa.a: As one friendly face in a class that was shutting him out; he happily shared his train maps.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel about going against the others?

qa.q: What did the coach do after watching?
qa.a: They spoke to the whole team about how to treat new players and paired Farhan and Tushar for drills.

qa.q: How might Farhan have felt when Tushar sat beside him at water break?
qa.a: Welcomed and less alone, happy enough to teach Tushar a word back.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy afraid to go against teammates who exclude a new player, yet including him quietly, which helps and shows courage.
